turns.prompt_text: Do you see these cable symbols Attached 1 file. - ee231127-9a7c-4360-958d-8bede4dfc516
turns.response_html:
Yes, I can see the cables in the image clearly. The symbols you are referring to—the dashed white/grey lines on one of the wires—are a common way for manufacturers to help you identify polarity or the neutral vs. hot wire.

In electrical and audio work, here is how those markings are typically interpreted across different communities and industries:

1. DC Power (Wall Adapters/Chargers)

In most small electronics (like the "wall wart" chargers for laptops or routers), a black cable with white dashed lines has a specific meaning:

  • Dashed/Striped Wire: Usually represents the Positive (+) connection.
  • Solid Black Wire: Usually represents the Negative (-) connection.
  • The Catch: Some manufacturers reverse this. If you are wiring a sensitive device, the most reliable way to check is with a multimeter.

2. Audio and Speakers

Audiophiles and professional installers use these marks to ensure "phase" (so all speakers move outward at the same time):

  • The Marked Wire: Generally treated as Positive (+) or the "red" terminal.
  • The Plain Wire: Treated as Negative (-) or the "black" terminal.
  • Pro Tip: It actually doesn't matter which you pick as long as you are consistent at both ends (e.g., if the dashed wire goes to the red terminal on the amp, it must go to the red terminal on the speaker).

3. Household Lamps (AC Power)

If this is a power cord for a lamp or a small appliance:

  • Dashed or Ribbed Wire: This is the Neutral wire. It should be connected to the wider blade of a plug and the silver screw of a light socket.
  • Smooth/Plain Wire: This is the Hot wire. It connects to the narrow blade and the brass screw.

What kind of device or project are you working on? Knowing that can help me give you more specific advice on which wire goes where.
